questions.q: In the worked example, what creates the Sentinel incident in the first place?
options: A phishing-report analytics rule fires when a user forwards a suspicious email
The playbook creates the incident as its first action
The automation rule creates the incident directly
An analyst manually types up the incident
questions.explain: A data connector plus an analytics rule turns the reported email into a Sentinel incident, before any automation rule evaluates it.

questions.q: What does the automation rule's condition check in this example?
options: That the incident has already been closed
That the playbook has run successfully at least once before
That the incident's analytics rule name matches the phishing-report detection
That the user's manager has approved the action
questions.explain: The condition scopes the rule so it only fires on incidents from the phishing-report detection, not unrelated alert types like brute-force logins.

questions.q: What are the playbook's three actions in this example, in order?
options: Run a KQL hunting query, create a bookmark, close the case
Escalate severity, email the CISO, isolate the device
Get incident details, post a message to Teams, add a tag to the incident
Disable the sender's account, delete the email, close the incident
questions.explain: The playbook pulls incident details, notifies the SOC channel in Teams, and tags the incident — it notifies and records, nothing more.

questions.q: What does this example's playbook deliberately NOT do?
options: Pull the incident's details for use in later steps
Auto-close the incident or take any action against the sender or the email
Add a tag back onto the incident
Post a message to a Teams channel
questions.explain: The playbook only notifies and tags — it doesn't decide the email is malicious or take a response action on that judgment.

questions.q: Why would this automation rule NOT fire on a brute-force login incident?
options: Because playbooks are hard-coded to ignore login-related incidents
Because the rule's condition checks for the phishing-report analytics rule name specifically, which a brute-force incident wouldn't match
Because brute-force incidents never get created in Sentinel
Because automation rules can only ever apply to one incident, ever
questions.explain: The condition is what keeps the rule scoped to exactly the incidents it's meant for — a non-matching incident simply never reaches the action.
